description: Frozen RFC 6962 / RFC 9162 Merkle test vectors for ATL Protocol implementations. Every value in this file has an origin recorded in `provenance`; none of them was produced by atl-core. A third-party implementation can be checked against this file without running, trusting, or even possessing atl-core.

provenance.why_this_matters: A test vector generated by the implementation it tests proves nothing: it freezes that implementation's bugs and then confirms them forever. Values here are therefore either published outside this project, or derived from RFC/specification text by an independent implementation (CPython `hashlib`), never by atl-core.

origins.rfc6962-published: Value belongs to the Certificate Transparency reference test-vector set that has circulated since 2013 with the CT reference implementation (google/certificate-transparency, test/merkletree_test.cc; mirrored in google/certificate-transparency-go, merkle/testonly). It was additionally reproduced here from the RFC 6962 Section 2.1 MTH definition by an independent implementation; the published value and the independent recomputation agree.
origins.rfc6962-symbolic: Structure (which nodes appear in a proof, and in what order) is stated symbolically in RFC 6962 Section 2.1.3 itself, using the node labels a..l of the 7-leaf diagram. See `rfc6962_section_2_1_3` below: the symbolic expectations printed in the RFC are reproduced exactly by the vectors in this file.
origins.rfc6962-derived: No published hex exists for this particular (index, size) pair. The value was computed from the RFC 6962 algorithm text -- Section 2.1 (MTH), Section 2.1.1 (PATH), Section 2.1.2 (PROOF/SUBPROOF), restated in RFC 9162 Sections 2.1.1, 2.1.3.1 and 2.1.4.1 -- by an independent implementation over CPython `hashlib.sha256`. It is checkable by re-deriving it from the RFC, not by running atl-core.

provenance.note_on_the_rfcs: Neither RFC 6962 nor RFC 9162 ships a table of hexadecimal test vectors; RFC 6962 Section 2.1.3 gives a worked example symbolically only. The hex values marked `rfc6962-published` come from the CT reference implementation, which is external to this project but is not an RFC. This distinction is deliberate and is the reason `rfc6962_section_2_1_3` is included: it is the one piece of proof structure that the RFC document itself pins down.

how_to_use.leaf_hashes_not_records: atl-core's Merkle functions consume leaf HASHES, not records: an ATL leaf hash is SHA256(0x00 || payload_hash || metadata_hash), i.e. RFC 6962's leaf rule applied to a 64-byte record. To replay these vectors, feed `records[].leaf_hash` (not `records[].data_hex`) into compute_root / verify_inclusion / verify_consistency.

definitions.split: k = largest power of two strictly smaller than n -- RFC 6962 Section 2.1

rfc6962_section_2_1_3.description: The 7-leaf tree drawn in RFC 6962 Section 2.1.3, with the RFC's own node labels bound to concrete hashes. The RFC states, in words: the audit path for d0 is [b, h, l]; for d3 is [c, g, l]; for d4 is [f, j, k]; for d6 is [i, k]; PROOF(3, D[7]) = [c, d, g, l]; PROOF(4, D[7]) = [l]; PROOF(6, D[7]) = [i, j, k]. Each of those symbolic statements is reproduced by the corresponding entry in `inclusion_proofs` / `consistency_proofs`, which carry a `rfc6962_2_1_3_labels` field for direct comparison.

j.definition: MTH(D[6:7]) = SHA256(0x00 || d6); the RFC diagram gives node j a single child d6
